title: Serbia Defies EU, President to Attend Putin's Victory Day Parade
text:
Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic is making headlines by defying EU pressure and planning a Moscow visit , a move that has important geopolitical implications. This article delves into the controversy surrounding Vucic’s decision, including the EU’s concerns, Serbia’s ties with Russia, and the domestic unrest brewing in Belgrade. Learn how this visit could impact Serbia’s future and its relations with the West as we unpack the story of vucic’s defiance of EU pressure .
Serbia’s Vucic Defies EU Pressure, Plans Moscow visit Amid Domestic unrest Defiance in the Face of Scrutiny Belgrade, Serbia – Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic has reaffirmed his intention to attend the Victory Day parade in moscow on May 9, despite mounting pressure from the European Union. The EU has cautioned that such a visit could jeopardize Serbia’s aspirations for membership in the bloc, potentially signaling a breach of accession criteria.
The planned attendance carries meaningful weight,effectively demonstrating support for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Moscow’s ongoing military actions against Ukraine. This decision arrives at a critical juncture as Serbia navigates its complex relationship with both the East and West.
EU Concerns and potential ramifications European officials have voiced strong disapproval of Vucic’s planned trip, emphasizing that it contradicts the principles expected of candidate countries. kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, articulated the bloc’s stance, stating they made it very clear that we do not want any candidate country to participate in these events on the 9th of May in Moscow. This firm position underscores the EU’s commitment to isolating Russia politically and diplomatically.
Despite claiming to seek EU integration, Vucic has maintained close ties with Russia, notably refusing to impose Western sanctions.This stance has significantly stalled Serbia’s accession talks with the 27-nation bloc, highlighting the challenges of balancing geopolitical interests.
Serbia’s Participation in the parade Adding to the controversy, Vucic announced that a Serbian military unit would participate in the May 9 parade on Red Square. He further stated that Serbia is, for the first time… taking part in “jointly” organizing the parade. This level of involvement signals a deepening of ties between Belgrade and Moscow, despite international condemnation of Russia’s actions.
Vucic acknowledged the anticipated scrutiny, telling reporters, In the coming period, we will be under pressure regarding the event in Moscow in which we have announced our participation. This statement suggests an awareness of the diplomatic tightrope he is walking.
Allied Support and Divergent Views Vucic is expected to be joined in Moscow by Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico, a fellow right-wing leader. Fico has criticized Kallas’s warnings against attending the parade, deeming them disrespectful. Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik has also confirmed his attendance, further illustrating the divisions within Europe regarding relations with Russia.
Domestic Unrest and Political Challenges Vucic’s decision comes amid significant domestic challenges, including widespread student-led anti-corruption protests that have shaken his 13-year rule. These protests were triggered by the Nov. 1 rail station canopy collapse in Novi Sad, which resulted in 16 fatalities and has been linked to questionable dealings with Chinese and other construction firms.
Adding to the political turmoil, the Serbian parliament recently approved a new government filled with ministers openly opposed to the EU. Information Minister Boris Bratina, for example, was recently shown setting an EU flag on fire while chanting, we don’t want the EU, we want union with Russia. The previous government collapsed under the weight of the protests.
Dismissal of Sonic Weapon Allegations At the same news conference, Vucic addressed allegations that authorities used sonic devices against protesters on March 15 in belgrade. He cited a report by Russia’s FSB spy agency, which claimed that these reports were false.
The Russian FSB categorically concluded that there was no use of any sonic weapons, Vucic said,without providing details on the FSB’s investigation or methodology. Sonic weapons, which utilize sound waves to incapacitate individuals, are sometimes employed for crowd control.
